918.title: Namdev and the Dog
918.hook: a saint chases a thief with butter, and a temple turns around
918.carry: the same Lord in the dog and the priest
918.tomorrow: Why would a saint split his last stalk with the wife who hit him?
918.howItsDone: Varkari devotees in Maharashtra sing Namdev's songs to Vitthal, and Sikhs read and sing the hymns under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib. Many Hindu homes, especially in north India, set aside the first roti for a cow and the last for a dog.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev, called half-baked by a potter, learned from Visoba Khechar's feet that there's nowhere without God.
screen: `NAMDEV.` · `NOWHERE TO PUT THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Lunch is laid out: a few pieces of flatbread, and a little pot of ghee, clarified butter, to spread on top. Namdev looks away for a moment. A stray dog trots in, snatches the bread, and runs. Namdev jumps up and goes after it. Not with a stick. He's carrying the pot of ghee, calling: wait, that bread is dry, let me butter it for you. That's the story told about him.
screen: `A DOG STEALS THE BREAD.` → `NAMDEV CHASES IT.` → `HE'S CARRYING THE GHEE.`

segments.voice: Visoba taught Namdev that there's no place without God. Here is that lesson trotting off on four legs. In the story, Namdev sees Vitthal in the dog, and the one problem left is that the bread is dry. Now a harder story. Namdev goes to a temple to sing; tradition places it at Aundha. The priests push him out. In their eyes, a man of his birth doesn't belong there. So Namdev walks around to the back, sits on the ground, and keeps singing. And the story says the temple turned, the whole building swinging around until its door faced Namdev. Namdev tells this one himself, in a hymn kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs: driven out for the community he was born into, he sang, and the temple turned to face him. Put the two stories side by side, and you have one of Hinduism's great teachings. The Bhagavad Gita says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the one the world calls an outcast. Teachers call it sama-darshana, the equal eye: one Lord living in every being. Namdev lived both halves of that verse. He saw God in the dog, and the story says God would not keep his back to a singer the priests saw as less. It's part of why many Hindu homes, especially in north India, still set aside the first roti for a cow and the last for a dog. The hungry animal at the door isn't outside the sacred.
screen: `THE LESSON ON FOUR LEGS.` · `THE TEMPLE TURNS.` · `A HYMN IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.` · then, large: `THE EQUAL EYE: ONE LORD IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, set a little aside, the way many Hindu homes keep a roti for the cow and one for the dog: a bite of bread, a handful of rice. Put it out for a bird or a neighbor's dog, or into the hands of someone who needs it. As you do, think of someone who annoyed you lately: the same Lord lives there too. If you pray, offer the food to God first; if you don't, simply give it with care.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur who chased a dog to butter its bread, and whose hymn of the turning temple is kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Your line: the same Lord in the dog and the priest. That's the Gita's equal eye, and Namdev chased it down the road with ghee. Day nine hundred eighteen, done.

919.title: Tukaram's Sugarcane
919.hook: a saint gives away his sugarcane, and his wife breaks the last stalk on his back
919.carry: it's all the Lord's, even the last stalk
919.tomorrow: What would you do if you were told to drown your songs?
919.howItsDone: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Namdev chased a dog with the butter, and sang behind a temple until, the story says, it turned to face him.
screen: `NAMDEV.` · `THE BUTTER, NOT THE STICK.`

segments.voice: A man walks home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. You peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up. Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then the next, and the next. By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, with a household to feed. The man is Tukaram.
screen: `AN ARMFUL OF SUGARCANE.` → `THE CHILDREN ASK.` → `ONE STALK LEFT.`

segments.voice: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river, a devotee of Vitthal, the same god Namdev sang to. Tradition says Namdev came to him in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs. Tradition says his shop failed and famine took people he loved, and out of that grief he turned his whole life toward Vitthal. Back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is furious. The story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away. She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me. It's funny. It's also an old Hindu teaching, lived with a stick of cane. The Isha Upanishad opens by saying that all this, everything that moves in the world, is dwelt in by the Lord. So enjoy it by letting go, and don't grasp: whose is the wealth, anyway? Nothing Tukaram holds is his. It's Vitthal's, passing through his hands, to the children, and then to the wife who's angry with him. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane. His Varkari tradition holds up exactly this: a householder with debts and a hungry family, singing to Vitthal in the middle of it.
screen: `A GROCER OF DEHU.` · `THE STALK SNAPS IN TWO.` · `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.` · then, large: `ALL THIS IS THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Before you eat today, pause over the plate, the way many Hindu families offer food to God before a meal and then eat it as prasad, a gift given back. Say inwardly, this is yours, Lord, or simply, this isn't only mine. Then think of one thing you've been gripping, and ask Tukaram's question: whose is it, really? If you don't pray, hold the plate a moment in thanks.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.
screen: `TUKARAM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it's all the Lord's, even the last stalk. Tukaram held nothing as his own, so even a broken stalk got shared. Until tomorrow.

920.title: The Notebooks in the River
920.hook: a grocer is told to drown his songs, and does
920.carry: God hears the language of home
920.tomorrow: Why would a weaver lie down where his teacher would step?
920.howItsDone: Varkaris sing Tukaram's abhangs in kirtan and on the yearly walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, when a palanquin carrying his sandals travels from Dehu with the pilgrims.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram split the last broken stalk of sugarcane with his wife. One for you, one for me.
screen: `TUKARAM.` · `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Indrayani, a man holds a bundle of handwritten notebooks full of songs. He steps to the edge and lets them go. They sink into the brown water and are gone. Nobody stole them or tore them up. He was told to do this, and he did it himself. Then he sits down on the bare ground by the water, and he doesn't get up.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF NOTEBOOKS.` → `INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE SITS DOWN ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: The songs are abhangs, the short devotional verses of the Varkari saints, made to be sung in Marathi, the everyday language Jnaneshwar had already opened the Gita in. Tukaram made them for Vitthal, and people sang them. Not everyone was pleased. Tradition names a learned man, Rameshwar Bhatt, who objected that a grocer had no business composing songs about sacred things, and in everyday Marathi at that. The story says he ordered Tukaram to sink his notebooks in the river. And Tukaram did. He doesn't argue, hide a copy, or run to another town. He obeys, then sits on the bank and refuses food, turning it all over to Vitthal. If the songs were his, let them drown. If they were Vitthal's, let Vitthal decide. Days go by. Then, tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface of the Indrayani, dry. The story goes one step further: the man who gave the order fell ill, and was healed only after he came to Tukaram and became his follower. It isn't told as a victory over an enemy, but as two people both changed by the songs. Here is the teaching. For centuries much sacred learning was kept in Sanskrit, by the learned. The bhakti saints sang to God in the languages their mothers spoke, Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, and their songs teach that God hears those just as well. Varkaris still sing Tukaram's abhangs. In the season of the great walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, a palanquin carrying his sandals sets out from Dehu, and the pilgrims sing his Marathi words along the road.
screen: `ABHANGS, IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `SINK THEM IN THE RIVER.` · `THE NOTEBOOKS RISE.` · then, large: `GOD HEARS THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.`

segments.voice: Pick one short prayer or line you already know: a mantra, a line from a bhajan, a grace before meals. Say it once as you learned it. Then say what it means in your own everyday language, slowly, as if speaking to someone right beside you. That's what Tukaram's abhangs did. If you don't pray, say the words you'd most want someone to hear, in your own tongue.

921.title: Kabir at the Guru's Feet
921.hook: a weaver lies down in the dark where his teacher will step
921.carry: bow low; the ego is the wall
921.tomorrow: Can a man who never learned to read be the real scholar?
921.howItsDone: Kabir's dohas are sung and quoted by followers of the Kabir Panth, in Hindu devotional singing, and in everyday talk; his verses are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. Touching an elder's or teacher's feet is a common Hindu sign of respect and humility.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram sank his notebooks in the Indrayani and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose dry.
screen: `TUKARAM.` · `THE NOTEBOOKS RISE.`

segments.voice: Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a famous teacher, Ramananda, comes down here to bathe at this hour. The teacher's foot comes down on him. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man goes home holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose. That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE GANGES.` → `A FOOT IN THE DARK.` → `RAM, RAM.`

segments.voice: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima. He wanted Ramananda as his guru, and how he got him is the lesson. He didn't argue his way in. He lay down lower than the step, where the teacher's foot would land, and took the name that came with it, Ram, as his whole teaching. In Hindu life, the feet are where you meet a teacher. Children touch their elders' feet; students bow at a guru's feet. Many explain it the same way: you lower your head, and the 'I' gets smaller. Hindu teachers have a word for that 'I': ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker. Many bhakti teachers picture it as a wall between a person and God. Kabir put the turn in a doha, a two-line rhyming couplet. This one begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. Roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and couldn't find anyone. Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Notice the trap. The first line is the ego's favorite hunt: who's the problem here? Found nobody. The second line turns the lamp around. It isn't saying you're terrible. It's the same move as lying on the step: get lower than your own 'I'. The ego hunts outside; humility looks in. That's where Kabir says the work is, and where there's room for God.
screen: `A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `UNDER THE GURU'S FOOT.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · then, large: `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: The next time you greet an elder, a grandparent or a teacher, try the old gesture of pranam: a bow, folded hands, or touching their feet if your family does. If not, simply bow your head inwardly. Then bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming, and turn Kabir's lamp around: what did I bring to this? If you pray, offer what you found to God; if you don't, let your 'I' be a little smaller for a minute.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi who got his guru by lying under his feet, and whose doha turns the hunt for the bad one back on the hunter.
screen: `KABIR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bow low; the ego is the wall. Kabir lay down under his teacher's foot, and found the bad one in his own heart. See you tomorrow.

922.title: Two and a Half Letters
922.hook: a weaver's two-line answer to a shelf of books
922.carry: bhakti: love, not books, makes the pandit
922.tomorrow: Why does a deer search the forest for a scent it carries?
922.howItsDone: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's first doha. I went looking for the bad one, found no one, then searched my own heart.
screen: `KABIR.` · `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: A shelf sags under the weight of books, commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask. Down the lane, a weaver throws the shuttle back and forth at his loom. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf, about how much reading it takes to become wise. His count is very small.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `A WEAVER AT HIS LOOM.` → `A VERY SMALL COUNT.`

segments.voice: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua. A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one became a pandit, a truly learned one. Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters is the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page. The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. Kabir doesn't say books are bad; his own verses ended up in books. He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. This is the heart of bhakti, the path of devotion all this week's saints walked. In their teaching, God is reached by prem, love, and love can't be finished on paper. A grandmother who sings to Ram with her whole heart may have read more of it than the man with the shelf. And here's the trap, like yesterday's. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line asks something of them too. Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them. In Kabir's picture, love of God is the text, every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.

923.howItsDone: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away; quietly repeating a name of God, like Ram, is a common Hindu practice; and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

segments.voice: A deer moves through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree. Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer. It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's the third doha this week, and the last day with the weaver of Kashi.
screen: `A SCENT IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE.` → `THE DEER KEEPS SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. Roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest. Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place. This is one of Hinduism's great teachings: God isn't only far away, in a temple or a heaven. God dwells within. In Hindi, God is often called antaryami, the one who lives inside and knows the heart. Kabir's Ram, the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi, isn't held in one temple or one image. Put the three dohas together. Go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Read book after book, and the lesson is still two and a half letters, love. Search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites. When they lifted the sheet, there was no body, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half, and honored him in its own way. Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, whose scripture keeps his verses, still honor him today: one saint, remembered by different paths with different rites.
screen: `THE MUSK IS IN THE DEER.` · `RAM IN EVERY HEART.` · `ANTARYAMI: THE ONE WITHIN.` · then, large: `ONLY FLOWERS UNDER THE SHEET.`

If you don't pray, rest on the words already here instead.

924.title: Tulsidas Bows First
924.hook: a husband crosses a flood at night, and his wife sends him to Ram

924.howItsDone: Hindus who love Ram read and sing the Ramcharitmanas at home and in temples, sometimes all the way through over several days, and its verses are chanted and staged in Ram Lila performances.

segments.voice: It's night, and the river is high from the rains. A young man comes home to find his wife gone to her parents' house across the water, and he can't stand to wait until morning. So he crosses the swollen river in the dark and climbs up to her window. She is not charmed. She's embarrassed, and tells him so, sharply: if you loved Ram the way you love this body of flesh and bone, you'd be free. The young man goes away and doesn't come back. That's how tradition tells the turning of Tulsidas.
screen: `A SWOLLEN RIVER AT NIGHT.` → `HIS WIFE'S SHARP WORDS.` → `HE TURNS TO RAM.`

segments.voice: Tulsidas became a poet of Ram, and his great work is the Ramcharitmanas, the story of Ram retold in Awadhi, a language people spoke, not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana. Like Namdev, Tukaram and Kabir this week, he sings in the language of home. But first he bows. The poem opens with a short run of Sanskrit verses, and the very first one bows to Vani, the goddess of speech, and to Vinayaka, Ganesha: makers of letters and meanings, of the flavors and meters of verse, and of everything auspicious. That opening bow has a name: mangalacharan, the auspicious beginning. It's why so many Hindu beginnings look the same: a puja that opens with Ganesha's name, a wedding card with Ganesha at the top, a new notebook marked Shri Ganeshaya Namah. Ganesha clears the road; the goddess of speech gives the words. Before a single word of his own, the poet thanks both. Tulsidas says why he writes: for the happiness of his own heart, svantah sukhaya. Not for fame. And the poem explains its own name. It says Shiva composed this story first and kept it in his own mind, his manas, so it's called the Manas of Ram's deeds. A man once turned around by his wife's sharp words begins his life's work with a bow, thanking the givers of words, and passing on a story Shiva held in his heart.
screen: `THE MANAS, IN AWADHI.` · `A BOW TO VANI AND VINAYAKA.` · `FOR MY OWN HEART'S JOY.` · then, large: `MANGALACHARAN: BEGIN WITH A BOW.`

segments.voice: Before the next thing you start today, a page, a message, a task, pause for an opening bow. Many Hindus say or write Shri Ganeshaya Namah, a bow to Ganesha, or ask Saraswati for the right words. Say it softly, or touch the page and ask for a clear road and good words. If you don't pray, name one thing you're grateful for before you begin, and start for the joy of it.
Tulsidas. The poet of the Ramcharitmanas, who bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at its door, and wrote the story of Ram for the happiness of his own heart.
